One of the narratives I see people trying to push again on here is memes, and I'm seeing comparisons to 2023. 

I don't see that at all. In 2023 memes were a kind of reaction to the low float high FDV VC scams that had been forced on the market.

They made "sense" as a counter movement to bring order and "fairness" (of course they weren't that fair) back to the market.

It was also the first time the technology got good enough where anyone could create tokens with no real technical expertise and we had a proper scalable L1 in Solana for the first time, so we had a few things combining to create the conditions for an explosion.

Look, I know memes will stick around in one form or another, and are kind of impossible to kill due to the lottery nature and return profile. There will always be a market for lotteries and hope (I'm not bearish Pump at these levels for this reason). 

But, there seems to be nothing new to the approach right now? People are citing that old memes will run again (conditions don't support this), and new ones are reliant on "attention", which is always fleeting. There are no new mechanisms here. We still haven't managed to nail social tokens as a result.

Memes can have a run again in a new bull market if we have excessive liquidity, but this isn't a new narrative to dramatically usher in a new crypto bull run with new entrants. 

You can't continue to play the same game where the end outcome is known by all the existing players, with far fewer players and no new entrants, and expect different results. 

This is the definition of madness.

tweets.text: On this day in 1914, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, the opening move of the First World War and the trigger for one of the fastest financial panics Wall Street had ever seen. Foreign investors, mostly British, began dumping roughly $3 billion of American securities to raise cash for the war, and prices buckled. The Dow had already slid about 11% in a month, and on its final session, July 30, it fell nearly 6.5% before officials pulled the plug. The New York Stock Exchange shut its doors on July 31 and stayed closed for more than four months, the longest suspension in its history, while London closed the same day for the first time ever. The pound spiked from $4.87 to nearly $6.75 as the world scrambled for gold. The war that began that day ended the first era of globalization and shifted the center of world finance from London to New York, where it has stayed ever since.

For sure, happy to expand. FWIW in relation to the assets you're talking about yeah the Chinese undercutting is def the vast majority of attribution.

As for monetary policy, it's not just the one rate change that is in question right now, there's multiple:

- FFR changes don't impact things as much when rate expectations are already in line with the move. When it's 99% odds and it goes in that direction, the change is small. However this time, and moving forward, it's 50/50 which means regardless of what happens tomorrow it will be a not fully priced change to the path of rate expectations.

- It's that path of rate expectations that is the crux here not just the one move. Without forward guidance and if they hike tomorrow, there is a good chance that the market will extrapolate that into a series of multiple rate hikes since the market has less to go on. 

- This delta of rate expectations impacts two things: changes in rate expectations do impact the long end of the yield curve. One model for a 10y bond is the present value of 10 years of the fed funds rate. So as that gets repriced, the long end gets repriced. Because hyperscalers have tapped their free cash flow, their main method for funding buildout is in corporate bond issuance. Corporate bond issuance pricing is anchored to the long end bond + a default risk. As yield curve goes up, the cost of issuance will go up making the economics of issuance more tenuous. 

- Increased rate volatility also has an impact on the cost of leverage for things like hedge funds and basis trade. This sits at the foundation of all risk assets since it is the funding leg of margin and leverage into risky assets. Higher variance here = bigger haircuts = smaller position sizes.

Changes in rate EXPECTATIONS, not the realized move, is a major driver or risk assets. I once did an analysis on changes in rate expectations vs quarterly bitcoin returns and the correlation is very high. Attached below.

A 35% to 40% probably of a hike is justified. Sure they might raise rates this week, but there is going to be tension and lots of dissents. No hike this week and 50 might be on the table for September.

—-

Years of Trump bashing the Fed has changed them. 

Before everything revolved around the Chair and what they wanted. That is why Wall Street parsed every word and framed every decision around the Chair, their personality and what they believed. The other 11 voters did not matter and were expected to go along with the Chair.

This is not the case anymore.

The Fed is now like the Supreme Court, all independent voters and can out vote the Chair. And there is no more Forward Guidance (signaling what they are going to do.) this is why the probability of a hike tomorrow is 35% to 40%, the Chair could get outvoted and we have no “guidance” either way.
——

All of these changes are positive, and should be applauded. 

The root of many of the Fed’s problems were centered in too much power vested to one person (causing terrible “groupthink”). Additionally, forward guidance that amounted to promises of future moves encouraged too much speculation and leverage among financial institutions as they perceived lower risks creating moral hazards (Fed bailouts for bad decisions.).

These practices had to end.

In the meantime many of the hot takes about the Fed here should be filed under “historical viewpoints” and not “current monetary policy.”

Securitize has $4.11B of tokenized assets onchain, and only 0.7% of it gets used.

Maple is a fraction of that size, yet 62% of its assets are actually being lent, borrowed and used in DeFi.

That gap matters because the whole point of putting an asset onchain is for people to lend it, borrow against it and trade it.

RWAs are a $30B market now, and 87% of it is just sitting there doing nothing.

So I stopped caring about who has the longest asset list and started watching utilization, because it tells you way more than market cap.

Here's how the major platforms stack up:

• @Securitize leads institutional issuance at ~$4.11B onchain. Utilization? Only 0.7%.

• @OndoFinance is getting the widest range of assets into 10+ chains , still only ~2.7% in use.

• @maplefinance is smaller, but a much larger 62% of its assets is actually being lent, borrowed and used in DeFi.

Everyone else is basically at zero, so that's not Maple being slightly better, it's Maple running a completely different business.

• @RobinhoodCrypto has a different advantage altogether. It already owns the app, wallet and customer relationship, so it doesn’t need to find users after launching the product.

• Then there’s @HyperliquidX, which isn’t really focused on tokenizing the underlying asset. It’s letting people trade stocks, gold, oil and indices around the clock through perps.

The category split makes the difference even clearer.

Bonds and money-market funds make up ~$16.25B of the market, but only around 5% is active in DeFi.

Private credit is much smaller at ~$3.55B, yet roughly 61% is already being put to work.

So the filter for the whole sector now is who can get RWA assets into wallets, lending markets and trading venues where people actually use them.

And for the tokens, the question is even simpler: when all this activity happens, does any of the money reach holders?

Because an RWA platform can build a very good business without creating a particularly useful token.

Perpetual users aren't in the underlying market, betting in the official "casino".

They're the people standing around the blackjack table, betting with each other on what might happen at the table. 

TradeXYZ and other Perp venues go up to them, and offer to referee PvP bets.. for a fee of course.

Whenever you're about to trade a new RWA Perp, remember you aren't Selena Gomez at the blackjack table. You're in the crowd.

Non-consensus view: Interest rate decisions will matter less to bitcoin over the next five years than they did in the past fifteen.

Rationale: Throughout bitcoin's history, interest rates  swung wildly -- from 0% to 2.5% to 0% to 5% to 3.5%.  Changes have been measured in whole percentage points. But future changes seem likely to be more modest; the CME expects a 50bps rise over the next year.   

My guess is that the Warsh Fed will more closely resemble the Greenspan Fed from the mid-1990s than the Bernanke/Powell Fed we've had recently, with small tweaks in rates. 

If that turns out to be true, the impact of rates will be smaller because the scale of changes will be smaller. Rates will still matter, of course, but other factors will be more important.
